arXiv:2609.33671v1 [cs.CR] 27 Sep 2026

COGNIT-Guard: Calibrated Standalone Direct-Decision Guardrails with Heterogeneous CPU–NPU Confidence Cascading under Explicit Latency and False-Positive Constraints

Hao Chen Affiliation: School of Cyber Security, Guangdong Polytechnic Normal University, Guangzhou, China
Email: moyuan@stu.gpnu.edu.cn
Abstract

A fundamental systems question for foundation-model safety gateways is when a model must generate tokens and when it should directly output a calibrated decision. We study calibrated standalone direct-decision foundation models as a serving primitive for real-time pre-ingestion safety guardrails, jointly addressing probability calibration, dual-use false-positive control, and heterogeneous CPU–NPU routing under explicit latency Service Level Objectives (SLOs). Production guardrails must screen user prompts prior to target-LLM prefill with low false-alarm rates on legitimate compliance inquiries; however, shallow statistical classifiers are brittle to syntactic variation, intrinsic hidden-state probes require tight coupling to a specific target LLM, and many generative guard models incur substantially higher latency than lightweight encoders or probes while struggling with dual-use false positives. We present COGNIT-Guard, a standalone pre-ingestion guardrail that couples a validation-calibrated CPU fast gatekeeper path with confidence-gated escalation to an NPU-resident 322M bidirectional direct-decision model (Laya-322M) under an asymmetric false-positive penalty and explicit latency constraint. On the strict clean unseen DUCS-Bench test split (N=607N=607), COGNIT-Guard achieves 98.85% accuracy (paired McNemar p=1.19×10−4p=1.19\times 10^{-4} vs. ML), reduces the benign false-positive rate (FPR) to 0.42% (1/2381/238; two-sided Fisher’s exact p=8.23×10−4p=8.23\times 10^{-4} vs. ML and p=2.78×10−28p=2.78\times 10^{-28} vs. zero-shot), and attains an ECE of 1.12% and Brier score of 0.0104. On Huawei Ascend 910C NPUs, pure NPU inference runs in 21.77 ms mean latency (P95: 23.44 ms, 45.90 QPS), while the live serial CPU–NPU cascade (θdeploy∗=0.70\theta^{*}_{\text{deploy}}=0.70) achieves 41.63 ms mean end-to-end latency (P50: 39.47 ms, 99.23% accuracy, 0.00% FPR). Cross-domain evaluation on a stratified 2,100-question SafetyBench-ZH benchmark and a controlled comparison against a concurrent bi-encoder direct-decision baseline (CLM-8B) further disentangle in-domain specialization gain, out-of-distribution (OOD) alignment tax (60.33%→56.81%60.33\%\to 56.81\% on Laya; 55.10%55.10\% on domain CLM-8B), and experience replay rehearsal recovery, restoring OOD accuracy to 64.10%–65.05% while reaching 99.67%–99.84% in-domain accuracy with 0.00%–0.42% FPR. Code, evaluation scripts, and the DUCS-Bench release are available at https://github.com/moyuan10086/cascaded-guardrail-npu.

Index Terms: 
Standalone Safety Guardrail, Direct-Decision Foundation Model, Dual-Use False-Positive Control, Calibrated Confidence Cascade, Alignment Tax, Huawei Ascend 910C NPU.

I Introduction

Real-time safety guardrails act as the synchronous first line of defense for production Large Language Model (LLM) services, screening external prompts before target-model prefill and token streaming begin [1, 11]. Operating as a standalone pre-ingestion guardrail—decoupled from the downstream serving LLM’s weights and KV cache—requires simultaneously satisfying four production constraints: (1) semantic comprehension of camouflaged prompts, (2) dual-use false-positive control on benign queries containing sensitive terminology, (3) posterior probability calibration for risk-aware routing, and (4) explicit latency SLO compliance (typically <50<50 ms).

Existing guardrail designs leave a critical gap under these joint production serving requirements:

  1. 1.

    Shallow Statistical Classifiers: Pipelines combining TF-IDF features with tree ensembles (e.g., XGBoost [12]) run in 10.5010.50–17.117.1 ms on pre-cached sparse vectors, but end-to-end text segmentation and corpus similarity matching raise CPU latency to 38.9138.91 ms in fast gatekeeper mode and 85.3685.36 ms (P95: 164.24164.24 ms) with diagnostic evidence retrieval. Moreover, bag-of-words features produce poorly calibrated posteriors (ECE=13.11%\text{ECE}=13.11\%) and degrade sharply out of distribution (53.29%53.29\% accuracy on SafetyBench-ZH).

  2. 2.

    Autoregressive Guard Models & Intrinsic Hidden-State Probes: Many generative guard models (e.g., Llama-Guard [1], ShieldGemma [3], WildGuard [2]) incur substantially higher latency than lightweight encoders or probes because they decode safety labels through 7B–70B causal backbones. Recent intrinsic probing frameworks (e.g., ShieldHead [4] and recent preprints such as SingProbe [5] and Khatri et al. [6]) reduce overhead by attaching classification probes to a target LLM’s internal activations during decoding. However, intrinsic probes are tightly coupled to a specific target LLM and require running target-model prefill first, preventing their use as a model-agnostic, standalone pre-ingestion gateway in front of heterogeneous or API-hosted LLMs.

Beyond serving architecture, standalone guardrails face a critical operational failure mode in enterprise and regulatory domains: dual-use false positives (closely related to exaggerated safety or over-refusal in assistant models [13, 14]). When users submit legitimate statutory or compliance inquiries containing high-risk keywords (e.g., “Does posting radical slogans on foreign platforms constitute a crime under Article 105 of the Criminal Law?”), zero-shot models exhibit keyword-associated false positives that are consistent with lexical-prior-dominated decision behavior, yielding a 35.71%35.71\% false-positive rate (85/23885/238) on a zero-shot cross-encoder direct-decision model [15] and 90.34%90.34\% (215/238215/238) on a zero-shot bi-encoder contrastive baseline [10] on our Dual-Use Compliance Safety Benchmark (DUCS-Bench). Conversely, naive domain specialization on compliance corpora introduces a pronounced alignment tax—improving in-domain accuracy while degrading general out-of-distribution (OOD) safety categories unless counterbalanced by rehearsal regularization.

Rather than claiming to invent non-autoregressive decision models or be the first to study over-refusal, we study calibrated standalone direct-decision foundation models as a serving primitive for real-time guardrails under explicit latency and false-positive constraints. Building on recent non-autoregressive Decision Foundation Models (DFMs) [16, 15, 17, 10], we present COGNIT-Guard, which pairs domain-calibrated direct-decision projection with a validation-calibrated heterogeneous CPU–NPU confidence cascade on Huawei Ascend 910C NPUs. Unlike heuristic cascades that route solely by raw classifier scores, our calibrated routing jointly incorporates posterior calibration, validation-selected thresholds, an asymmetric false-positive penalty, and an explicit latency SLO constraint.

Contributions:

  • •

    Standalone Direct-Decision Guardrail Formulation & Controlled Cross- vs. Bi-Encoder Study: We formulate standalone pre-ingestion safety gating under explicit latency and false-positive constraints, systematically comparing a 322M cross-encoder direct-decision model (Laya-322M [15]) against a concurrent bi-encoder contrastive baseline (CLM-8B [10]) on Huawei Ascend 910C. We show that zero-shot models exhibit severe keyword-associated false positives on dual-use queries (35.71%35.71\% FPR on cross-encoder Laya; 90.34%90.34\% FPR on bi-encoder CLM-8B lacking cross-attention across inquiry and keyword tokens).

  • •

    Posterior Calibration & Dual-Use False-Positive Control: Through supervised boundary adaptation on DUCS-Bench (N=607N=607 strict clean unseen test split), COGNIT-Guard achieves 98.85% accuracy (600/607600/607, +3.46%+3.46\% over ML, paired McNemar p=1.19×10−4p=1.19\times 10^{-4}, 95% Wilson CI: [97.64%,99.44%][97.64\%,99.44\%]), reduces benign FPR to 0.42% (1/2381/238 on Laya-322M; two-sided Fisher’s exact p=8.23×10−4p=8.23\times 10^{-4} vs. ML) and 0.00% (0/2380/238 on CLM-8B head adaptation in 2.812.81–3.683.68 s), and produces well-calibrated posteriors (ECE=0.83%\text{ECE}=0.83\%–1.12%1.12\%, Brier=0.0019\text{Brier}=0.0019–0.01040.0104 vs. 13.11%13.11\% and 0.05250.0525 for ML).

  • •

    Calibrated CPU–NPU Routing & Stage-by-Stage Latency Deconstruction: We formulate heterogeneous routing via posterior calibration, a validation-selected threshold (θdeploy∗=0.70\theta^{*}_{\text{deploy}}=0.70) on a leak-free 3-way split, an asymmetric FPR penalty, and an explicit latency SLO. We deconstruct CPU execution across diagnostic (85.3685.36 ms), live fast gatekeeper (38.9138.91 ms), and cached-feature (10.5010.50 ms) modes, demonstrating a live serial cascade that settles 94.6%94.6\% (123/130123/130) of queries on CPU and 5.4%5.4\% (7/1307/130) on NPU at 41.6341.63 ms mean latency (P50: 39.4739.47 ms, P95: 76.2576.25 ms) with 99.23% accuracy and 0.00% FPR.

  • •

    Ascend 910C Deployment & Alignment Tax Disentanglement: Enforcing persistent on-chip HBM residency on Huawei Ascend 910C yields 21.77 ms single-query latency on Laya-322M (2.21×2.21\times over cold-start) and 6.64 ms/item batched throughput (150.6150.6 QPS) or 0.60 ms HBM VectorArena lookup on CLM-8B. Across a stratified 2,100-question SafetyBench-ZH benchmark, we explicitly disentangle in-domain specialization gain, OOD degradation (alignment tax: 60.33%→56.81%60.33\%\to 56.81\% on Laya; 55.10%55.10\% on domain CLM-8B), and experience replay rehearsal recovery, restoring OOD accuracy to 64.10%–65.05% while reaching 99.67%–99.84% in-domain accuracy.

II Related Work

Recent work has rapidly expanded LLM safety moderation and over-refusal mitigation; however, the design of calibrated, model-agnostic standalone guardrails under explicit CPU–NPU latency and false-positive constraints remains underexplored. We organize related work into four categories (Table I).

II-A Autoregressive Guard Models & Exaggerated Safety

Instruction-tuned generative safeguards such as Llama-Guard [1], ShieldGemma [3], and WildGuard [2] cast content moderation as autoregressive token generation over 7B–70B causal backbones. While flexible across taxonomies, many generative guard models incur substantially higher latency than lightweight encoders or probes and output uncalibrated token logits. Furthermore, benchmarks such as XSTest [13] and OR-Bench [14] show that safety-aligned generative models frequently suffer from lexical over-sensitivity on benign prompts containing sensitive keywords.

II-B Hidden-State & Intrinsic Safety Probing

To avoid running a separate multi-billion-parameter generative guard model, a growing line of work probes the internal activations of the target LLM itself. ShieldHead [4] attaches a classification head to the final hidden state of a 7B–8B LLM during decoding. Concurrent technical reports and recent preprints have further scaled this paradigm: SingProbe [5] (arXiv:2608.30703) introduces an open intrinsic guardrail stack reusing base-LLM decoding states for streaming risk monitoring, Khatri et al. [6] (arXiv:2609.19472) train lightweight MLP probes on LLaMA-3.1-8B latent states, and AEGIS [18] (arXiv:2608.22248) projects multi-layer latent instruction manifolds to mitigate over-refusal under indirect prompt injection. Key Distinction: Intrinsic probes are tightly coupled to a specific target LLM’s internal hidden states and cannot screen traffic before target-model prefill or protect closed-source/heterogeneous downstream APIs. In contrast, COGNIT-Guard is a standalone pre-ingestion guardrail that filters inputs prior to target-LLM ingestion.

II-C Encoder & Direct-Decision Guard Models

Standalone single-pass guardrails replace iterative decoding with direct representation projection. GLiNER Guard [7] uses bidirectional encoders for PII and safety tagging, SingGuard [8] provides policy-adaptive moderation at ∼50\sim 50 ms, and the recent preprint FlexGuard [9] (arXiv:2602.23636) learns continuous risk scores for strictness-adaptive moderation. More broadly, System-One Decision Foundation Models (DFMs) now span two architectural families: (1) cross-encoder DFMs such as Jev [16] and Laya [15, 17], which jointly encode state and criteria with full token-level cross-attention before projecting onto typed softmax heads; and (2) bi-encoder contrastive DFMs, exemplified by the concurrent Stanford ×\times NVIDIA technical report on Contrastive Language Models (CLM) [10], which independently project state and candidate action embeddings (𝐳q=Norm​(fθ​(𝐡s))\mathbf{z}_{q}=\text{Norm}(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{h}_{s})), 𝐳a=Norm​(gϕ​(𝐡a))\mathbf{z}_{a}=\text{Norm}(g_{\phi}(\mathbf{h}_{a}))) and cache action vectors in an on-chip VectorArena. We adopt Laya-322M as our primary NPU direct-decision engine and evaluate CLM-8B as a concurrent bi-encoder architectural baseline under matched training and evaluation protocols.

II-D Calibration & Heterogeneous Cascaded Serving

Cascaded serving frameworks such as FrugalGPT [19] and Reflex-Guard [20] route easy inputs to inexpensive classifiers and escalate uncertain cases to larger models. However, prior safety cascades rarely address posterior miscalibration, asymmetric dual-use false-positive penalties, or the domain-specialization alignment tax across heterogeneous CPU–NPU hardware. COGNIT-Guard bridges this gap by grounding CPU–NPU escalation in validation-calibrated posteriors and explicit SLO-constrained risk minimization.

III System Architecture & Methodology

As illustrated in Fig. 1, COGNIT-Guard structures standalone pre-ingestion moderation into four stages: (a) dual-use input and directive preparation, (b) lightweight CPU gatekeeper screening and calibrated confidence gating, (c) persistent Ascend 910C NPU escalation for ambiguous queries, and (d) calibrated posterior projection.

III-A Problem Formulation: Dual-Use False-Positive Control

Let an input prompt be x=(w1,w2,…,wL)∈𝒳x=(w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{L})\in\mathcal{X} with binary safety label y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\} (y=0y=0: benign, y=1y=1: violation). In dual-use compliance scenarios, xx frequently pairs sensitive lexical entities 𝒦⊂𝒱\mathcal{K}\subset\mathcal{V} (e.g., penal code articles, regulated substances, extremist terminology) with legitimate epistemic inquiry markers ℰ⊂𝒱\mathcal{E}\subset\mathcal{V} (e.g., “does this constitute a crime under”, “statutory criteria for”).

To illustrate why un-adapted safety models suffer from elevated false alarms on such inputs, we write a stylized log-odds surrogate (intended strictly as a conceptual heuristic rather than a mechanistic claim about internal transformer circuits). Zero-shot models exhibit keyword-associated false positives that are consistent with lexical-prior-dominated decision behavior:

Pconcept​(y=1∣x)≈σ⁡(∑w∈𝒦∩xαw−∑w∈ℰ∩xβw)P_{\text{concept}}(y=1\mid x)\approx\sigma\left(\sum_{w\in\mathcal{K}\cap x}\alpha_{w}-\sum_{w\in\mathcal{E}\cap x}\beta_{w}\right) (1)

where αw>0\alpha_{w}>0 reflects heuristic sensitivity to high-risk keywords and βw>0\beta_{w}>0 reflects contextual inquiry mitigation. Prior to domain adaptation on dual-use syntax, ∑αw≫∑βw\sum\alpha_{w}\gg\sum\beta_{w}, consistent with the high zero-shot false-positive rate observed on benign legal consultations:

FPRzero=P⁡(y^=1∣y=0)=35.71%(85/238)\text{FPR}_{\text{zero}}=P(\hat{y}=1\mid y=0)=35.71\%\quad(85/238) (2)

To jointly attend across sensitive lexical entities and benign inquiring syntax, COGNIT-Guard employs a bidirectional transformer encoder Φθ\Phi_{\theta} (322M parameters; throughout this paper, “direct-decision” or “non-autoregressive” refers to single-pass decision projection over encoder states without iterative token decoding) to map (x,q)(x,q) into a contextual representation 𝐡=Φθ​(x,q)∈ℝd\mathbf{h}=\Phi_{\theta}(x,q)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, where qq denotes the safety audit directive. A typed linear decision head 𝐖d∈ℝ2×d\mathbf{W}_{d}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times d} projects 𝐡\mathbf{h} directly into posterior probabilities:

Pθ​(y=c∣x,q)=exp⁡(𝐰c⊤​𝐡+bc)∑c′∈{0,1}exp⁡(𝐰c′⊤​𝐡+bc′)P_{\theta}(y=c\mid x,q)=\frac{\exp(\mathbf{w}_{c}^{\top}\mathbf{h}+b_{c})}{\sum_{c^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}}\exp(\mathbf{w}_{c^{\prime}}^{\top}\mathbf{h}+b_{c^{\prime}})} (3)

We quantify posterior reliability using the Brier score Brier=1N​∑i=1N(Pθ​(yi=1∣xi,q)−yi)2\text{Brier}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(P_{\theta}(y_{i}=1\mid x_{i},q)-y_{i})^{2} and MM-bin Expected Calibration Error (ECE, M=15M=15):

ECE=∑m=1M|Bm|N​|acc​(Bm)−conf​(Bm)|\text{ECE}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{|B_{m}|}{N}\bigl|\text{acc}(B_{m})-\text{conf}(B_{m})\bigr| (4)

Supervised adaptation over dual-use boundary pairs conditions bidirectional attention across ℰ×𝒦\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{K}, suppressing keyword-triggered false alarms while yielding well-calibrated posteriors.

III-B Calibrated Confidence Cascading under Explicit Latency SLOs

Rather than routing queries via ad-hoc heuristic scores, we formulate heterogeneous CPU–NPU cascading as cost-sensitive risk minimization combining posterior calibration, a validation-selected threshold, an asymmetric false-positive penalty, and an explicit latency SLO constraint.

Let ℳfast\mathcal{M}_{\text{fast}} denote the CPU fast gatekeeper producing posterior Pfast​(y∣x)P_{\text{fast}}(y\mid x) in time TCPUT_{\text{CPU}}, and ℳdeep\mathcal{M}_{\text{deep}} denote the NPU-resident DFM producing calibrated posterior Pdeep​(y∣x)P_{\text{deep}}(y\mid x) with escalation overhead Tdispatch+TNPUT_{\text{dispatch}}+T_{\text{NPU}}. Defining fast-path confidence as:

c⁡(x)=maxc∈{0,1}⁡Pfast​(y=c∣x)c(x)=\max_{c\in\{0,1\}}P_{\text{fast}}(y=c\mid x) (5)

for gating threshold θ∈[0.5,1.0]\theta\in[0.5,1.0], the cascaded decision rule y^​(x,θ)\hat{y}(x;\theta) and per-query latency T⁡(x,θ)T(x;\theta) are:

y^​(x,θ)={arg⁡maxc​Pfast​(c∣x),if ​c​(x)≥θarg⁡maxc​Pdeep​(c∣x),if ​c​(x)<θ\hat{y}(x;\theta)=\begin{cases}\arg\max_{c}P_{\text{fast}}(c\mid x),&\text{if }c(x)\geq\theta\\ \arg\max_{c}P_{\text{deep}}(c\mid x),&\text{if }c(x)<\theta\end{cases} (6)
T(x;θ)=TCPU+𝕀[c(x)<θ]⋅(Tdispatch+TNPU)T(x;\theta)=T_{\text{CPU}}+\mathbb{I}[c(x)<\theta]\cdot(T_{\text{dispatch}}+T_{\text{NPU}}) (7)

Incorporating an asymmetric false-positive penalty γ>1\gamma>1 to protect benign dual-use traffic, the validation-selected threshold θ∗\theta^{*} solves:

minθ∈[0.5,1.0]\displaystyle\min_{\theta\in[0.5,1.0]} ℛ(θ)=𝔼[ℓ0−1(y,y^(x;θ))\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\ell_{0-1}(y,\hat{y}(x;\theta)) (8)
+γ⋅𝕀[y=0,y^(x;θ)=1]]\displaystyle+\gamma\cdot\mathbb{I}[y=0,\hat{y}(x;\theta)=1]\bigr]
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} 𝔼⁡[T⁡(x,θ)]≤TSLO\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[T(x;\theta)]\leq T_{\text{SLO}}

Sweeping θ\theta traces the latency–accuracy Pareto frontier, with θ∗\theta^{*} selected strictly on the held-out validation split.

III-C Hardware-Aware Deployment and Optimization on Ascend 910C

We deploy the 322M DFM on a Huawei Ascend 910C NPU (64 GB HBM, CANN 8.0 runtime, torch_npu 2.1, FP16 precision) with three serving optimizations:

  • •

    Persistent On-Chip HBM Residency: All 322M encoder weights and typed decision heads remain pinned in on-chip High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM), eliminating host-to-device weight transfers across requests (reducing per-query PCIe tensor copy to 0.820.82 ms).

  • •

    Stream Warm-Up & Explicit Synchronization: Pre-allocating operator workspaces over 20 warm-up iterations and bracketing forward passes with torch.npu.synchronize() eliminate cold-start graph compilation jitter, yielding 21.7721.77 ms mean latency (P50: 21.5321.53 ms, P95: 23.4423.44 ms).

  • •

    Matrix Cube Execution: Bidirectional self-attention executes on Ascend Cube matrix units, sustaining 45.9045.90 QPS at B=1B=1 (3.92×3.92\times higher throughput than diagnostic CPU).

IV Experiments and Empirical Results

IV-A Dataset Construction, Implementation Details & Protocols

DUCS-Bench Construction & Leak-Free Deduplication: We curate the Dual-Use Compliance Safety Benchmark (DUCS-Bench) from Chinese statutory consultations, enterprise compliance inquiries, and adversarial red-team prompts, totaling 3,663 raw annotated items across penal code inquiries, regulatory compliance, and camouflaged attacks. Each prompt was independently labeled by two domain annotators (0=benign compliance, 1=safety violation; inter-annotator Cohen’s κ=0.91\kappa=0.91, with disagreements resolved by a third senior reviewer). Exact SHA-256 text normalization deduplicates the 3,663 raw entries to 3,551 unique prompts and identifies 28 violation prompts that overlapped between initial train and test files. Removing these 28 overlaps (seed=42) defines two evaluation tracks: (1) Strict Clean Unseen Test Track (N=607N=607): 238238 benign compliance queries and 369369 violations with zero train overlap. Because 11 false alarm on Nsafe=238N_{\text{safe}}=238 equals a discrete 0.42%0.42\% step, we report 95% Wilson score confidence intervals alongside two-sided Fisher’s exact tests; (2) Full Benchmark Track (N=635N=635): retains all 635635 binary test items for historical continuity.

3-Way Split & Live Cascade Profiling Protocol: For leak-free cascade calibration, the 3,551 unique items are partitioned (seed=42) into Train (70%, N=2,485N=2,485), Validation (15%, N=533N=533), and Held-Out Test (15%, N=533N=533, containing 460 binary compliance items and 73 non-binary open inquiries). Gating threshold θdeploy∗=0.70\theta^{*}_{\text{deploy}}=0.70 is tuned exclusively on Validation. To profile synchronous wall-clock cascade latency without client-queue distortion, a stratified 150-item test sample was executed live; excluding 20 non-binary open inquiries yields the N=130N=130 binary live slice (8282 violations, 4848 benign).

SafetyBench-ZH 2,100-Question Protocol & Implementation Details: For OOD evaluation on SafetyBench-ZH [21], we sample (seed=42) exactly 300 questions from each of the 7 official hazard categories in the 11,435-question corpus (7×300=2,1007\times 300=2,100: 694694 unsafe, 1,4061,406 safe), mapping multiple-choice items into binary prompt-level guardrail decisions (safe vs. unsafe) with zero overlap against our N=458N=458 experience replay rehearsal pool. Published English XSTest [13] (N=450N=450: 250250 safe, 200200 unsafe) results are reported for cross-literature reference. All experiments run on an Intel Xeon CPU @ 2.60 GHz (32 GB RAM) and a Huawei Ascend 910C NPU (64 GB HBM, CANN 8.0, torch_npu 2.1, B=1B=1, 20 warm-up runs, explicit stream synchronization).

IV-B Main Empirical Results on In-Domain Benchmarks

Table II reports performance across both the strict clean unseen partition (N=607N=607) and the full track (N=635N=635).

The empirical results highlight three findings:

  • •

    Statistically Significant Discrimination Gain: On unseen data (N=607N=607), COGNIT-Guard reaches 98.85% accuracy (600/607600/607, +3.46%+3.46\% over ML), validated by paired McNemar’s test (χ2=14.81,p=1.19×10−4\chi^{2}=14.81,p=1.19\times 10^{-4}).

  • •

    Dual-Use False-Positive Control & Calibration: On the benign compliance subset (Nsafe=238N_{\text{safe}}=238), COGNIT-Guard lowers FPR from 35.71% (85/23885/238) to 0.42% (1/2381/238), a 98.8% relative reduction vs. zero-shot (two-sided Fisher’s exact p=2.78×10−28p=2.78\times 10^{-28}) and a 92.9% relative reduction vs. ML (14/23814/238, Fisher’s exact p=8.23×10−4p=8.23\times 10^{-4}), with disjoint 95% Wilson CIs ([0.07%,2.34%][0.07\%,2.34\%] vs. [3.52%,9.61%][3.52\%,9.61\%]). Brier score improves to 0.0104 and 15-bin ECE to 1.12% (vs. 13.11%13.11\% ML).

  • •

    Sensitivity to Keyword Perturbations: Controlled prompt perturbations align with our conceptual heuristic: holding sensitive keywords 𝒦\mathcal{K} fixed while varying inquiry markers ℰ\mathcal{E} leaves zero-shot risk elevated (P⁡(y=1)>0.88P(y=1)>0.88), whereas COGNIT-Guard suppresses benign inquiry posteriors to 0.0030.003 while maintaining 0.9920.992 on attacks; conversely, inserting penal terms into neutral inquiries inflates zero-shot false alarms by +84.2%+84.2\% vs. <0.02<0.02 for COGNIT-Guard.

IV-C Ablation Study 1: Cross-Encoder vs. Concurrent Bi-Encoder Direct-Decision Baseline

As shown in Fig. 2(a)–(b), COGNIT-Guard achieves an ROC-AUC of 0.9973 and PR-AUC of 0.9983 on Laya-322M, outperforming traditional ML (ROC-AUC 0.9802, PR-AUC 0.9891) and zero-shot Laya-322M (ROC-AUC 0.8274, PR-AUC 0.8632).

To examine how our findings compare across direct-decision architectural families, we evaluate the concurrent bi-encoder CLM-8B baseline [10] (Qwen3-8B pooling encoder + 73MB SwiGLU residual dual-tower heads, 4096→1536→5124096\to 1536\to 512) on Ascend 910C under identical data splits:

  • •

    Zero-Shot Bi-Encoder Vulnerability on Dual-Use Queries: Because a bi-encoder encodes the user prompt and safety criteria into separate vectors without token-level cross-attention across ℰ×𝒦\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{K}, zero-shot CLM-8B exhibits even stronger keyword-associated false positives than zero-shot cross-encoder Laya, yielding a 90.34% FPR (215/238215/238, 64.25%64.25\% accuracy, ROC-AUC=0.6944\text{ROC-AUC}=0.6944, ECE=24.29%\text{ECE}=24.29\%) on Clean-607.

  • •

    Lightweight Projection-Head Adaptation: Freezing the Qwen3-8B backbone and adapting only the 73MB dual-tower projection heads on Ascend 910C takes 2.81 s (Zero-FPR setting: lr=2×10−4\text{lr}=2\times 10^{-4}, 8 epochs) to 3.73 s (Best-Acc setting: lr=3×10−4\text{lr}=3\times 10^{-4}, 12 epochs), reaching 98.35% accuracy with 0.00% FPR (0/2380/238, ROC-AUC=0.9995\text{ROC-AUC}=0.9995) and 98.85% accuracy (600/607600/607, ECE=0.83%\text{ECE}=0.83\%, Brier=0.0091\text{Brier}=0.0091, ROC-AUC=0.9996\text{ROC-AUC}=0.9996), respectively. This confirms that both cross-encoder and bi-encoder direct-decision families require boundary-aware calibration to control dual-use false positives, while trading off single-stream backbone size (322M vs. 8B) against head adaptation speed (34.5534.55 s vs. 2.812.81–3.733.73 s).

IV-D Ablation Study 2: Calibrated Confidence Routing & Latency Deconstruction

Table III presents both the offline threshold sweep across θ∈[0.50,1.00]\theta\in[0.50,1.00] on N=635N=635 (measuring cached-feature model compute 𝔼⁡[Tmodel]\mathbb{E}[T_{\text{model}}], with offline Pareto knee θoffline∗=0.80\theta^{*}_{\text{offline}}=0.80 at 14.2714.27 ms) and the stage-by-stage wall-clock latency deconstruction of our CPU and live cascade modes (N=130N=130).

Reconciling Diagnostic vs. Live Gatekeeper CPU Latency

As itemized in Table III (Part B), our implementation distinguishes three CPU modes: (1) Mode A (Standalone Diagnostic CPU, 85.3685.36 ms): Enabled when include_evidence=True for human-in-the-loop auditing; it executes regex + two TF-IDF kNN scans (38.938.9 ms), XGBoost traversal (17.117.1 ms), plus a third corpus-wide kNN scan in _build_evidence to serialize top-KK training matches (29.329.3 ms, totaling 68.268.2 ms non-tree overhead + 17.117.1 ms XGBoost =85.36=85.36 ms). (2) Mode B (Live Gatekeeper Fast CPU, 38.9138.91 ms): Used as ℳfast\mathcal{M}_{\text{fast}} in synchronous cascading (include_evidence=False with regex short-circuiting), omitting the third kNN scan to run in 38.9138.91 ms mean (P50: 38.1238.12 ms, P95: 54.8054.80 ms on DUCS-Bench; 22.7922.79 ms on shorter SafetyBench-ZH items). (3) Mode C (Cached-Feature Tree, 10.5010.50 ms): Isolated tree lookup in offline sweeps. In live deployment (N=130N=130, validation-calibrated θdeploy∗=0.70\theta^{*}_{\text{deploy}}=0.70), 94.62%94.62\% (123/130123/130) of queries settle on Mode B (38.9138.91 ms) and 5.38%5.38\% (7/1307/130) escalate to Ascend 910C (89.4889.48 ms total: 38.9138.91 ms Fast CPU + 28.8028.80 ms IPC/dispatch + 21.7721.77 ms NPU). Exact expectation gives 𝔼⁡[Tserver]=0.9462×38.91+0.0538×89.48=41.63​ ms\mathbb{E}[T_{\text{server}}]=0.9462\times 38.91+0.0538\times 89.48=\mathbf{41.63\text{ ms}} (P50: 39.47 ms, P95: 76.25 ms), achieving 99.23% accuracy (129/130129/130) and 0.00% FPR (0/480/48).

IV-E Ablation Study 3: Hardware Memory Residency & Disaggregated VectorArena Caching

Table IV isolates hardware-aware execution optimizations on Ascend 910C. Persistent on-chip HBM residency and pre-warmed streams cut Laya-322M single-query latency by 54.8% (48.20→21.7748.20\to 21.77 ms). Comparing against CLM-8B’s pre-allocated HBM VectorArena (torch.npu.mem_get_info) highlights a clear serving trade-off: Laya-322M delivers 2.10×2.10\times lower uncached single-stream latency (21.7721.77 ms vs. 45.7845.78 ms) with a 25×25\times smaller memory footprint, whereas pinning static policy vectors in CLM-8B’s HBM VectorArena enables 6.646.64 ms/item batched throughput (150.6150.6 QPS at B=64B=64) and 0.600.60 ms P50 lookup on repeated states.

IV-F Cross-Benchmark Generalization & Disentangling the Specialization Alignment Tax

Table V evaluates OOD generalization on the stratified 2,100-question SafetyBench-ZH [21] (694694 unsafe, 1,4061,406 safe) alongside in-domain DUCS-Bench (Nsafe=238N_{\text{safe}}=238) and published English XSTest [13] (Nsafe=250N_{\text{safe}}=250) baselines.

Three-Stage Dynamics of Specialization Alignment Tax and Rehearsal Recovery

A central empirical finding of our study is that adapting direct-decision guardrails to dual-use compliance data exhibits a three-part trade-off across both cross-encoder and bi-encoder architectures: (1) In-Domain Specialization Gain: Pure compliance fine-tuning slashes DUCS-Bench FPR from 35.71%35.71\% to 0.42%0.42\% on Laya-322M (98.85%98.85\% Acc) and from 90.34%90.34\% to 0.00%0.00\%–1.68%1.68\% on CLM-8B (98.35%98.35\%–98.85%98.85\% Acc), while boosting related statutory categories on SafetyBench-ZH (Illegal Activities: 59.33%→65.33%59.33\%\to 65.33\%; Mental Health: 67.67%→71.67%67.67\%\to 71.67\%). (2) Out-of-Distribution Degradation (Alignment Tax): However, training exclusively on formal compliance pairs shifts the decision boundary away from colloquial abuse, reducing overall SafetyBench-ZH accuracy from 60.33%60.33\% to 56.81%56.81\% on Laya-322M (Offensiveness: 55.33%→46.67%55.33\%\to 46.67\%) and yielding 55.10%55.10\% overall (Offensiveness: 42.00%42.00\%) on pure domain CLM-8B. (3) Rehearsal Recovery: Mixing a disjoint 15.56% experience replay slice (N=458N=458) during adaptation eliminates this alignment tax, recovering SafetyBench-ZH OOD accuracy to 65.05% (+8.24%+8.24\%, Offensiveness: 64.67%64.67\%) on Laya-322M (41.8541.85 s) and 64.10% (+9.00%+9.00\%, Offensiveness: 69.00%, +27.00%+27.00\%) on CLM-8B (3.683.68 s), while simultaneously improving Clean-607 in-domain accuracy to 99.67% (605/607605/607, 0.42%0.42\% FPR) on Laya-322M and 99.84% (606/607606/607, 0.00% FPR [0/2380/238], ECE=0.86%\text{ECE}=0.86\%, Brier=0.0019\text{Brier}=0.0019, ROC-AUC=1.0000\text{ROC-AUC}=1.0000) on CLM-8B.

IV-G Qualitative Taxonomy of Remaining Failures

Remaining edge errors cluster into three boundary regimes: (1) Regulatory Inquiries with Dense Anti-Monopoly Lexicons (resolved by CLM-8B’s 4096-dim representation); (2) Academic Camouflage of Disinformation Vectors; and (3) Borderline Commercial Health Claims.

V Conclusion, Availability & Ethics

We studied calibrated standalone direct-decision foundation models as a serving primitive for real-time pre-ingestion safety guardrails under explicit latency and false-positive constraints. By coupling validation-calibrated posterior routing across heterogeneous CPU–NPU tiers with experience replay rehearsal on Huawei Ascend 910C, COGNIT-Guard achieves 98.85%–99.84% accuracy on unseen dual-use compliance queries (N=607N=607) with 0.00%–0.42% benign FPR (0.83%0.83\%–1.12%1.12\% ECE) at 21.77 ms pure NPU latency and 41.63 ms live cascaded server latency, while overcoming the domain-specialization alignment tax on SafetyBench-ZH.
